glossary.program: A list of steps for the rover to do, one after another.
glossary.run: Make the rover do the program.

intro:
This is a program.
It is a list of steps for the rover.
This one has one step: drive 1 metre.
Press Run and watch the rover do it.
Then change 1 to 2 and Run it again.
solutionCode: move_forward(2)
starterCode: move_forward(1)
title: Watch It, Then Change It

glossary.forward: Go straight ahead, the way the rover is facing.
glossary.program: A list of steps for the rover to do, one after another.

intro:
Let's drive the rover!
Each line tells the rover one thing to do.
The rover does them in order, from the top.
Right now it only drives 1 metre, which is not far enough.
The flag is 3 metres straight ahead.
Change the number, or add another line, to reach it.
solutionCode:
move_forward(1)
move_forward(1)
move_forward(1)
starterCode: move_forward(1)
title: Drive to the Flag

glossary.turn: Spin on the spot to face a new way. The rover does not move forward while turning. A quarter turn is 90 degrees, like turning to face the next wall of a room.

intro:
The flag is not straight ahead this time.
It is around a corner.
The rover must drive, make a quarter turn to the left,
then drive again.
turn_left(90) is a quarter turn.
solutionCode:
move_forward(2)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(2)
starterCode: move_forward(2)
title: Turn the Corner

glossary.loop: A way to repeat the same steps again and again, without writing them out each time.
glossary.turn: Spin the rover to face a new direction, measured in degrees.

intro:
A square has four equal sides.
Instead of writing the same steps four times, we use a loop.
"for side in range(4):" repeats the lines below it four times.
Below is ONE side. Wrap those two lines in a for loop
so the rover repeats them and draws the whole square.
starterCode:
move_forward(2)
turn_right(90)
title: Make a Square

glossary.if: Do something ONLY when a question is true.
glossary.obstacle: A rock or wall in the way that the rover must not hit.
glossary.sensor: A part that lets the rover measure the world around it, like its eyes.

intro:
A clever rover looks before it moves.
"obstacle_ahead()" asks the sensor a yes/no question:
is there a rock right in front of me?
Press Run first and watch the rover hit the rock.
Then add "if obstacle_ahead():" and a turn ABOVE the move,
so it looks before it drives.
starterCode: move_forward(3)
title: Look Before You Move

glossary.bug: A mistake in a program that makes it do the wrong thing. Finding and fixing bugs is called debugging.

intro:
Another engineer wrote this program, but it has a bug.
The rover should go around the rock to the flag,
but it turns the WRONG way and crashes.
Press Run and watch where it goes wrong.
Then fix ONE word and run it again.
solutionCode:
move_forward(1)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(2)
starterCode:
move_forward(1)
turn_right(90)
move_forward(2)
title: Fix the Broken Program

intro:
Welcome to Kodro. Your first job is to give the rover three
instructions in order: drive forward, beep, and write a short message
to the console. This is called a "sequence".
The rover does not drive far enough yet. Change the number in
move_forward so it travels at least 1.5 metres, then run it again.
solutionCode:
move_forward(2)
beep(1)
log("hello rover")
starterCode:
move_forward(1)
beep(1)
log("hello rover")
title: Hello, Rover!

intro:
The rover can do more than drive forwards. Use turn_left and turn_right
to change its heading. Build a short path that ends at the sample patch.
solutionCode:
move_forward(3)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(3)
collect_sample()
starterCode:
move_forward(3)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(3)
title: Move and turn

intro:
Drive a U-shaped path: forward, turn, forward, turn, forward. Then
collect the sample at the far end. Every line of your program is one
step in the sequence.
The last move stops short of the sample, so nothing is collected.
Work out how far that last move needs to be.
solutionCode:
move_forward(3)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(2)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(3)
collect_sample()
starterCode:
move_forward(3)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(2)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
title: Sequence

intro:
A rock sits between the rover and the sample patch.
The starter program already asks the sensor whether something is in the
way, and drives round it when the answer is yes.
Run it and watch: the rover ends up right on the patch, but comes home
empty. Add the one line that picks the sample up.
solutionCode:
if obstacle_ahead(2.0):
    turn_left(90)
    move_forward(1)
    turn_right(90)
    move_forward(4)
    turn_right(90)
    move_forward(1)
    collect_sample()
starterCode:
if obstacle_ahead(2.0):
    turn_left(90)
    move_forward(1)
    turn_right(90)
    move_forward(4)
    turn_right(90)
    move_forward(1)
title: Selection (if / else)

glossary.boolean: A value that is either True or False. Sensor questions like obstacle_ahead() answer with a boolean.

intro:
This program was meant to be careful: check for a rock,
and turn away if one is there. But the test is BACKWARDS,
so the rover turns only when the path is clear, and drives
straight into the rock when it is not.
Run it, read the if line closely, and fix the condition.
title: Fix the Backwards Test

intro:
Drive forward and collect samples while avoiding rocks. Use a while loop
so the rover keeps moving until it sees an obstacle, then turn and
continue. Every loop iteration is one step.
solutionCode:
turn_left(30)
while not sample_detected():
    move_forward(0.2)
collect_sample()
turn_right(45)
while not sample_detected():
    move_forward(0.2)
collect_sample()
turn_left(40)
while not sample_detected():
    move_forward(0.2)
collect_sample()
title: Iteration with while-loops

intro:
Wrap the "drive then turn" pattern in a function so you can call it many
times. Functions let you give a meaningful name to a sequence of
instructions -- this is called "decomposition".
solutionCode:
def hop():
    move_forward(2)
    collect_sample()
    turn_left(90)

hop()
hop()
hop()
hop()
starterCode:
def hop():
    move_forward(2)
    turn_left(90)

hop()
hop()
hop()
hop()
title: Functions

intro:
Underwater visibility is poor. Combine read_distance() with a while loop
so the rover stops one metre before any wall, no matter how far it is.
starterCode:
while read_distance() > 1.0:
    move_forward(0.5)
title: Reading sensors

intro:
A rock sits between the base and the sample.
The starter program already gets there. It keeps driving while it cannot
see the sample, and when the sensor says something is in the way it calls
dodge() to step around it.
Then it stops, and the mission is not finished until the rover is home.
Turn it around and write the same loop again for the journey back.
You do not need to write dodge() a second time. That is what a function is for.
starterCode:
def dodge():
    turn_left(90)
    move_forward(1.5)
    turn_right(90)
    move_forward(2)
    turn_right(90)
    move_forward(1.5)
    turn_left(90)

while not sample_detected():
    if obstacle_ahead(1.0):
        dodge()
    else:
        move_forward(0.5)

collect_sample()
title: Pathfinding basics

intro:
Draw a square spiral by calling a function that calls itself with a
smaller step. Recursion lets you describe an infinite-looking pattern
with just a few lines of code -- the base case stops the spiral.
Call pen_down() first if you want the rover to leave a trail as it goes.
The spiral drives the same shape either way, so the pen is yours to choose.
solutionCode:
def spiral(step):
    if step < 0.5:
        return
    move_forward(step)
    turn_left(90)
    spiral(step - 0.5)

pen_down()
spiral(3.0)
starterCode:
def spiral(step):
    if step < 0.5:
        return
    move_forward(step)
    turn_left(90)
    spiral(step - 0.5)

spiral(1.0)
title: Recursion (KS4 stretch)

intro:
Three samples are scattered across the arena. Collect them all using the
smallest possible distance travelled. Try a couple of orderings and keep
the cheapest one -- this is the simplest form of route optimisation.
solutionCode:
# Order 3-2-1 costs 22 m of driving, but 1-3-2 costs 28 m, so drive 3-2-1.
for _ in range(6):
    move_forward(1)
turn_left(90)
move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
for _ in range(3):
    move_forward(1)
turn_left(90)
for _ in range(2):
    move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
for _ in range(3):
    move_forward(1)
turn_right(90)
move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
turn_left(90)
move_forward(1)
turn_left(90)
for _ in range(5):
    move_forward(1)
starterCode:
# First pass: walk to each sample, collect it, head home.
# Sample 1 at (2, 6): turn north, go 5, collect.
turn_left(90)
for _ in range(5):
    move_forward(1)
turn_right(90)
move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
# Sample 2 at (5, 5): south + east a bit.
turn_right(90)
move_forward(1)
turn_left(90)
for _ in range(3):
    move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
# Sample 3 at (7, 2): south then east.
turn_right(90)
for _ in range(3):
    move_forward(1)
turn_left(90)
for _ in range(2):
    move_forward(1)
collect_sample()
# Return to base.
turn_left(180)
for _ in range(10):
    move_forward(1)
title: Optimisation (KS4 stretch)

intro:
Break the patrol into named jobs. Write one small helper function per
leg of the route, then call them in order. Decomposition turns a single
long problem into a few short ones you can read and test on their own.
solutionCode:
def leg_one():
    move_forward(3)
    collect_sample()

def leg_two():
    turn_left(90)
    move_forward(3)
    collect_sample()

leg_one()
leg_two()
starterCode:
def leg_one():
    move_forward(3)
    collect_sample()

def leg_two():
    turn_left(90)
    move_forward(3)
    collect_sample()

leg_one()
# TODO: call leg_two() so the rover reaches the second sample too
title: Decomposition (KS4 stretch)

glossary.read_battery: Reports how much charge is left, from 100 (full) down to 0 (flat).

intro:
Don't hard-code the route -- ask the world. The starter drives blindly
and crashes. Use obstacle_ahead() to decide when to turn, so one short
program copes with whatever is in the way. Reading a sensor is an
abstraction: you get "is something there?" without caring how it is
measured. The loop keeps going while read_battery() is above 40, so the
mission stops itself before the rover runs flat.
title: Abstraction (KS4 stretch)

intro:
Sweep the whole field, not just one row. The starter collects a single
row of samples; wrap it in a second loop so the rover repeats the sweep
for every row. A loop inside a loop is "nested iteration" -- the inner
loop runs in full on each pass of the outer loop.
solutionCode:
for row in range(2):
    for col in range(3):
        move_forward(2)
        collect_sample()
    # turn around at the end of the row and line up with the next one
    move_forward(2)
    turn_left(90)
    move_forward(2)
    turn_left(90)
starterCode:
# This sweeps ONE row. Wrap it in a second loop to cover every row.
for col in range(3):
    move_forward(2)
    collect_sample()
title: Nested loops (KS4 stretch)

intro:
Keep a running tally. The starter collects one sample and adds 1 to a
counter; turn it into a loop that repeats until the counter reaches the
target. A variable you add to on each pass is called an accumulator -- it
is how programs count things while they iterate.
solutionCode:
count = 0
while count < 3:
    move_forward(2)
    collect_sample()
    count = count + 1
starterCode:
# A counter variable, but no loop yet.
count = 0
move_forward(2)
collect_sample()
count = count + 1
# TODO: wrap the move/collect/count in a while loop until count == 3
title: Counting with a variable (KS4 stretch)

intro:
One function, many jobs. The starter's `hop` always moves the same fixed
distance, so it can only reach one sample. Give it a `distance` parameter
and call it with different values to reach every sample. A parameter is an
input that lets a single function be reused for different cases.
solutionCode:
def hop(distance):
    move_forward(distance)
    collect_sample()

hop(2)
hop(3)
hop(2)
starterCode:
# hop always moves 2m. Add a `distance` parameter and pass different values.
def hop():
    move_forward(2)
    collect_sample()

hop()
title: Functions with parameters (KS4 stretch)

glossary.collect_sample: Picks up the sample the rover is standing on. It is already written for you here.
glossary.sample: A marker on the ground for the rover to pick up. The flags in this lesson are samples.
glossary.variable: A name that remembers a value. Use the name and you get the value.

intro:
Two flags, and both are the same distance away: 2 metres east, then
2 metres north.
The program stores that distance in a variable called step, and uses the
name twice. Right now step is 1, which is too short for BOTH moves.
Change the number ONCE, and watch both moves change with it.
That is what a variable is for.
solutionCode:
step = 2
move_forward(step)
collect_sample()
turn_left(90)
move_forward(step)
collect_sample()
starterCode:
step = 1
move_forward(step)
collect_sample()
turn_left(90)
move_forward(step)
collect_sample()
title: One name, used twice

intro:
Three sample patches sit along this track, at different spacings: 2 metres,
then 1 more, then 3 more.
You could write six lines of drive-and-collect. Instead, put the three
distances in a list and let one loop walk it. The DATA describes the route;
the code just follows the data.
The starter's list is wrong. Fix the numbers, not the loop.
solutionCode:
steps = [2, 1, 3]
for step in steps:
    move_forward(step)
    collect_sample()
starterCode:
steps = [2, 2, 2]
for step in steps:
    move_forward(step)
    collect_sample()
title: A list drives the route
